title: Hybrid Custom and Synthesized Logic Methodology
decision: Used a hybrid approach: custom circuit design for performance-critical macros (caches, FPUs, crosspoints) and automated logic synthesis for control and non-critical logic.
alternatives_or_rejected: Full-custom design was rejected due to the massive transistor count and time-to-market constraints; full-synthesis was rejected as it could not meet the aggressive frequency targets.
rationale: To balance the need for high clock frequency and performance with the practical limits of design manpower and schedule.
outcome: Successfully achieved high-frequency operation while managing design complexity and schedule for the 174-million-transistor die.
weakest_point: The exact phrasing of the frequency target or the exact list of custom vs synthesized blocks.

title: Hierarchical Partitioning for Timing Closure
decision: Partitioned the chip into a hierarchy of manageable physical blocks (macros) with strict interface timing budgets to enable parallel physical design and timing closure.
alternatives_or_rejected: Flat physical design and timing analysis was rejected because the massive die size exceeded the capacity of flat EDA tools and would not allow parallel team execution.
rationale: Necessary to handle the massive design size, enable parallel work by multiple design teams, and achieve timing closure within the project schedule.
outcome: Enabled concurrent design of multiple processor cores and large shared caches on a single die, achieving timing closure.
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly uses the term 'flat physical design' as the rejected alternative or just implies it by describing the hierarchical flow.

title: Global and Local Clock Distribution Grid
decision: Implemented a global clock distribution network to distribute the clock to local macro grids, minimizing clock skew across the large multi-core die.
rationale: The large die size and high operating frequency made clock skew a dominant timing challenge; a grid structure provides robust, low-skew clock delivery despite process and load variations.
outcome: Achieved tight clock skew control across the multi-core die, enabling correct synchronous operation at high frequencies.
weakest_point: The exact terminology (whether they call it a 'global grid', 'clock mesh', or 'H-tree to local grids') used in the paper for the top-level clock structure.

title: Dense Power Grid for di/dt Noise Mitigation
decision: Designed a dense, multi-layer power and ground grid (mesh) across the chip to minimize IR drop and inductive di/dt noise.
rationale: The simultaneous switching of multiple high-performance cores and large caches created massive transient current demands that could cause fatal voltage droop without a robust power grid.
outcome: Maintained stable supply voltage margins across the die during worst-case switching scenarios, preventing timing failures due to power noise.
weakest_point: The specific metal layers or exact density metrics mentioned in the paper for the power grid.

title: Wire Delay Modeling and Repeater Insertion
decision: Utilized systematic methodologies and automated tools for inserting repeaters (buffers) into long global and semi-global copper interconnects to manage RC wire delays.
alternatives_or_rejected: Manual repeater insertion was rejected as impractical due to the sheer volume of long wires and the iterative nature of physical placement and routing.
rationale: In the copper technology node, wire RC delays became comparable to or exceeded gate delays, making systematic repeater insertion critical for timing closure on long routes.
outcome: Successfully managed long-wire delays across the large die, allowing global communication between cores and cache interfaces to meet cycle time targets.
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly highlights 'automated repeater insertion' as a specific methodological decision or just discusses wire delay modeling and buffering generally.
